A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SMART research work. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, support reliable comparison after matching relocated and renumbered content.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations on four aerodynamic datasets, architectural ablations, query-distribution tests, and quantitative and qualitative predictions in Section 5 and Appendices K–L.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds sampling, shape-generalization, inference-cost and Transolver++ comparisons in Appendices K–L.

M1.justification: SMART's architecture, positional encoding, cross-layer interactions, loss and training/inference procedure remain unchanged. Farthest-point sampling is tested as an ablation; uniform sampling remains the proposed default, and v1 already mentioned alternative sampling strategies.

E1.justification: Appendix L.1.6 adds actual training and evaluation on SHIFT-SUV fastback vehicles and an estate-to-fastback transfer scenario. v1 restricted its SHIFT-SUV experiments to the estate subset. The original four benchmarks and mesh/query-shift scenarios are retained.

E2.justification: v2 adds Transolver++ to an actual full-resolution comparison on AhmedML, SHIFT-SUV and SHIFT-Wing (Table 27), reporting out-of-memory failures on an A100 80GB GPU. v1 discussed Transolver++ but did not evaluate it. The existing comparison methods are retained.

E3.justification: New experiments compare uniform versus farthest-point sampling during training and inference, introduce estate-trained and fastback-trained controls, and measure inference on five million query points. These are additional protocols; the existing experiments' splits, metrics, training budgets and tabulated model configurations are unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds a targeted sampling-sensitivity ablation (K.6), a shape-category distribution-shift test (L.1.6), and computational profiling (L.1.7). These extend the analysis without replacing the existing component ablations, mesh/query robustness tests or qualitative cases.

E5.justification: Both versions describe multiple initializations and report means and standard deviations for the matched experiments; those entries are unchanged. No new seed counts, significance tests or uncertainty-estimation procedures are specified. The new timing result includes a ± quantity but no additional run-count information.

E6.justification: Existing benchmark and component-ablation scores are unchanged. New results show small sampling differences (Table 19), estate-to-fastback errors 82–84% higher for surface prediction and 167–168% higher for volume prediction than fastback-trained controls (Table 26), and 17.11±0.0656 seconds for the five-million-query timing workload. Transolver++ memory failures and SMART resource measurements are added. Figure 19(c) also revises the displayed SHIFT-Wing drag values while retaining R² = 1.00.

T1.justification: Appendix B adds an explicit quantified definition of query independence and a short argument that pointwise query operations and read-only cross-attention satisfy it. This formalizes the earlier verbal treatment; the existing model equations, training objective and force calculations remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list and conclusion retain the same claims about mesh-free prediction, independent queries, cross-layer geometry–physics interaction and competitive accuracy. The additional experiments do not revise these principal claims.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly acknowledges that SMART does not enforce conservation laws and interprets the transfer experiment as evidence of unreliable generalization to unseen shape categories. It also adds flow-based reasoning for latent-size selection and recommends uniform sampling based on its cost and similar accuracy. The earlier domain, temporal and sampling limitations are retained.

D1.justification: New Appendix J explains how latent geometry size should reflect domain extent and flow structure. Appendix L.1.7 documents the timing workload, model configuration, precision and hardware. Existing hyperparameter tables, training-time information and code-access statement are unchanged; the code statement is merely relocated.

R1.justification: The cited work set is retained, with bibliographic updates to existing references. However, L.1.8 adds explicit scalability positioning against Transolver++, contrasting SMART's reported 7GB memory use with an extrapolated multi-GPU requirement. v1 only described Transolver++ in related work.

P1.justification: The limitations discussion moves from Appendix A to main-text Section 6, and appendix sections are correspondingly renumbered. v2 adds localized explanatory paragraphs and analysis subsections and updates publication information. Most existing prose and the central narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 19, 26 and 27, reflows existing tables and figures, and redraws Figure 19(c) with different drag-axis ranges. The existing benchmark displays, architecture diagrams and qualitative examples are substantially retained; later table numbering changes largely reflect the inserted sampling table.

improvement.justification: The new shape-transfer failure makes applicability limits clearer, while sampling checks and inference measurements provide useful evidence for practical use. Explicitly acknowledging the absence of conservation constraints also improves transparency. These are limited gains: the conclusion still claims reliability across all tested scenarios despite the new transfer limitation, and the Transolver++ multi-GPU requirement is extrapolated rather than measured.
